title: Isle of Skye
text: Of Skye, a rugged island on the west coast of the Scottish Highlands, the following notice has lately been made in a Perth newspaper: -"The years are but comparatively few since there were no roads in Skye, and, conse- quently, no conveyances, such as carts, gigs, vehicles, &c., which are now as numerous as in any other country. Travelling was then no less arduous than dangerous; and at many times it could not be at all effected, when the mountains poured down their rapid torrents into the contracted valleys underneath. But the case is now otherwise. The whole isle is intersected with beautiful roads. Its rivers and rivulets are severally crossed with substantial bridges. The good Hebridean has no longer to guess the distance which he walks, or to form his long Highland miles in imagination. His ways are marked and measured with firmly-fixed hewn granite mile-stones, and each stone is formed into three faces, on which are figured the distances from localities of importance. The march of improvement is equally apparent in the postoffice department. At present, the mails arrive from the Scottish metropolis three times a-week, at the remotest corner of Skye, in the space of about forty-eight hours. Let this be contrasted with the state of letter-conveyance less than half a century ago, as many in the place still freshly recollect. There were then no public roads be tweet Skye and Inverness, and, consequently, no mail-gigs or post-horses as at present. How, then, it may be asked, were the letters carried? They were conveyed from the Highland capital to Skye, and vice versa, by a sturdy Hebridean, who was hired for the purpose by the resieach trip. Owing to the great distance to be performed, gentlemen, at the low rate of about five shillings for to the want of public roads, and the difficulties of the Journey, Norman's visit from Inverness could hardly be Looked for more frequently than twice a-month or so."
